b.t: Read each section slowly, out loud. German spelling is much more regular than English spelling: once you know the rules in section 1.4, you can pronounce almost every word correctly the first time you see it. That is why this book starts with sounds before grammar.

Every German sentence has a speaker button, and a small slow button next to it that plays it at a slower pace. At the top of the page you can choose a male or a female voice and switch the English translations on or off. A good habit: cover the translation, read the German, then check.
At the end of each section you will find exercises. They tell you why an answer is right or wrong, so do not skip the explanations. They are part of the lesson.
Anna and Raj meet on the first day of a German course in Berlin. Read the dialogue once for meaning, then again aloud.
Anna and Raj meet at the entrance of the language school.
Anna: Hallo! Ich heiße Anna. Und du?
b.g: Hi! My name is Anna. And you?

b.t: Raj: Hallo, Anna. Ich heiße Raj.
b.g: Hi, Anna. My name is Raj.

b.t: Anna: Woher kommst du, Raj?
b.g: Where do you come from, Raj?

b.t: Raj: Ich komme aus Indien. Und du?
b.g: I come from India. And you?

b.t: Anna: Ich komme aus Deutschland. Wie geht's?
b.g: I come from Germany. How are you?

b.t: Raj: Gut, danke. Und dir?
Anna: Auch gut. Tschüss, Raj!
Raj: Tschüss, Anna! Bis morgen!

Three things to notice before we go on. First, there is no word for "am" in "my name is": German says Ich heiße Anna, literally "I am-called Anna". Second, du is used between two students: it is the informal "you". Third, Wie geht's? is short for Wie geht es dir?, literally "How goes it to you?". You will see why it is dir and not du when we meet the dative case later in the book.
German greetings depend on the time of day and on how formal the situation is.

r: during the day; polite and neutral
only when someone is going to bed
formal; literally "until we see each other again"

b.t: Merke: Gute Nacht is not "good evening". It means goodnight and is only said when parting for the night. If you meet someone at 8 p.m., say Guten Abend.
Achtung: In writing, the greeting is capitalised: Guten Morgen. Greeting words are not a place where English helps you: there is no German word for "good afternoon". Use Guten Tag until the evening.

Regional greetings are worth recognising even if you do not use them yet. In northern Germany you will hear Moin at any time of day. In Bavaria and Austria people say Servus and Grüß Gott, and in Switzerland Grüezi. All of them mean "hello".
Guten Morgen, Frau Weber!
Guten Tag, Herr Patel.
Guten Abend!
Gute Nacht, Anna!
Hallo, wie geht's?
Auf Wiedersehen!
Tschüss, bis morgen!
Bitte, danke, Entschuldigung
Three little words do a lot of work in everyday life.
• danke means "thank you". The polite reply is bitte.
• bitte has two jobs: it means "please" when you ask for something, and "you're welcome" when you answer danke. English needs two words; German uses one.
• Entschuldigung means "excuse me" (to get attention) and "sorry" (for a small mistake). For something more serious, say Es tut mir leid, "I'm sorry".
Einen Kaffee, bitte.
Danke! – Bitte!
Entschuldigung, wie bitte?
Ja, bitte.
Nein, danke.
Tipp: When you do not understand something, say Wie bitte? ("Pardon?"). It is polite and every German speaker understands it immediately.

b.t: German is spelled much more consistently than English. Learn the rules below once and you can read aloud almost anything, even words you do not understand yet. Keep in mind that the English comparisons are approximations: always listen to the 🔊 buttons too.
The alphabet
German uses the same 26 letters as English, plus ä, ö, ü (called Umlaute) and ß (called Eszett or "scharfes S").
To spell a word aloud, say the letter names in a row. On the phone you will also hear spelling words ("A wie Anton"), but the plain letter names are enough for now.
Vowels: long or short
Every vowel has a long and a short version. The rule of thumb that works most of the time:
• A vowel is long before one consonant, before h, or when it is doubled: Name /ˈnaːmə/, Sohn /zoːn/, Tee /teː/.
• A vowel is short before two or more consonants: Land /lant/, kommen /ˈkɔmən/, Mutter /ˈmʊtɐ/.
The h after a vowel is silent. It only tells you the vowel is long: Zahl /tsaːl/, Uhr /uːɐ̯/.

r: Land (a short "ah", like "u" in "cup" but clearer)
Tee like "ay" in "say", without the y
Brot like "oh" in "go", without the w

b.t: An unstressed e at the end of a word is a soft "uh", as in the "a" of "about": Name /ˈnaːmə/, bitte /ˈbɪtə/.
The umlauts ä, ö, ü
These three sounds do not exist in English, so they are worth practising.
• ä is almost the same as short e: Männer, Käse. When it is long it sounds like the "e" in "pet" held longer: Käse /ˈkɛːzə/.
• ö: say "eh" and round your lips as if saying "oh". It sounds a bit like the vowel in "bird" with no r: schön /ʃøːn/, Köln.
• ü: say "ee" and round your lips as if saying "oo". für /fyːɐ̯/, Tschüss /tʃʏs/, grün.
If your keyboard cannot type them, write ae, oe, ue instead (schoen, Tschuess) and ss for ß. Native speakers do exactly this in emails and passwords.
The letter ß
ß is simply a double s. It appears after long vowels and diphthongs: heißen /ˈhaɪ̯sn̩/, Fuß, groß. After a short vowel you write ss: Wasser, muss. There is no capital ß in everyday writing.
Diphthongs
Four vowel pairs are single sounds and are the source of many beginner errors. Learn them by the second letter in the pair:

Achtung: ei and ie are mirror images and sound completely different. ei is "eye": nein means "no" and sounds like "nine". ie is "ee": Wie sounds like "vee". Many learners mix up Wein (wine) and wie (how). The second letter tells you the sound.
Consonants that surprise English speakers

r: sp, st at the start of a word
ch after e, i, ä, ö, ü, ei, eu
ch after a, o, u, au
harsh, from the back of the throat, like the Scottish "loch"
usually a soft throaty sound; after a vowel at the end of a word it is a faint "uh"

b.t: The two sounds of ch are really one letter pair with two neighbours: the ich-sound after "front" vowels and the ach-sound after "back" vowels. A good test is the pair ich / ach: say them one after another and feel where your tongue is.
Merke: Final devoicing. At the end of a word, b, d, g are pronounced as p, t, k: Tag /taːk/, und /ʊnt/, Land /lant/, ab /ap/. In the plural the sound returns: Tage /ˈtaːɡə/.
Where is the stress?

Almost every German word is stressed on the first syllable: Ma-ma, Na-me, Ta-ge. There are two common exceptions you will meet early: words that begin with be-, ge-, ver-, er- put the stress on the next syllable (be-zah-len, Ge-mü-se), and many words borrowed from French or Latin are stressed late (Stu-dent, Tele-fon).

Kultur: Landeskunde: where is German spoken? German is the official language of Germany, Austria and Liechtenstein, and one of four official languages in Switzerland (alongside French, Italian and Romansh). It is also spoken in parts of Italy (South Tyrol), Belgium and Luxembourg. Each region has its own greetings and accent, but the written standard you are learning is the same everywhere.
Learn the nouns with their article and plural. The vocabulary also appears in your Glossar, where you can review it with flashcards.

The same question, Wie heißen Sie? or Wie heißt du?, can sound very different depending on who you are talking to. Read both dialogues aloud, then notice how every verb changes.

b.g: Good day. My name is Raj Patel.

b.t: Herr Patel: Ich komme aus Indien. Und Sie?
b.g: I come from India. And you?

b.t: Frau Weber: Ich komme aus Österreich, aber ich wohne in Berlin.
b.g: I come from Austria, but I live in Berlin.

Raj: Ich heiße Raj. Und du?

What changed between the two conversations? Sie with -en verbs (heißen Sie, kommen Sie, sprechen Sie) versus du with -st verbs (heißt du, wohnst du). The rest of the chapter explains why, one piece at a time.

pages.t: K2 · 2.2 Personal pronouns: who is doing it?

b.t: A pronoun replaces a noun. If you say Anna wohnt in Berlin. Sie ist Studentin., the word sie replaces Anna. German chooses the pronoun by person (first, second, third), number (one or more) and, for the third person, gender.
Four points are worth a closer look.

1. ich is not capitalised unless it begins a sentence. Du and ihr are written with small letters in normal text. 2. German has two kinds of "you" for one person (du and Sie) and one extra for several people (ihr). English you covers all of them. 3. Sie (formal "you") is always written with a capital S, in every position in the sentence. That is the main way to tell it apart from sie (she, they) on the page. 4. sie has three meanings: she, they and (capitalised) Sie = formal you. In speech they sound identical. The verb ending tells you which one it is:
Sie kommt aus Indien.
Sie kommen aus Indien.
b.g: They come from India. / You (formal) come from India.

b.t: Kommen Sie aus Indien?

pages.t: K2 · 2.2 Personal pronouns: who is doing it? (2)

b.t: Merke: Grammatical gender and natural gender are different things. er, sie, es replace nouns by their grammatical gender, not only by the sex of a person. A table is der Tisch, so you say er for it. You will learn how to find a noun's gender in chapter 3. For now, use er for a man, sie for a woman and es for a child or a thing like das Auto ("it").
This is the first real cultural decision a learner has to make, and it is easier than it sounds.
• Use du with friends, family, children, pets, fellow students and, in many workplaces and clubs, colleagues. Online, du is the standard.
• Use Sie with strangers, officials, shop staff, your teacher, your boss and anyone older than you whom you do not know well.
• If in doubt, use Sie. Nobody will mind that you are too polite. Being too casual to a stranger can sound rude.
• The switch to du is usually offered by the older or more senior person: Wollen wir uns duzen? ("Shall we use du?"). It is also fine to ask.
• Sie goes with Herr/Frau + surname: Frau Weber, Herr Patel. Du goes with first names.

Kultur: Moving from Sie to du is a small social event in German-speaking countries. People sometimes celebrate it with a drink: das Du anbieten, "to offer the du". Don't be surprised if a colleague uses du from day one: many start-ups, universities and Scandinavian-style companies do. When you meet someone in a shop, at the post office or on the phone for the first time, Sie is the safe choice.

pages.t: K2 · 2.4 Verbs: the infinitive, the stem and the endings

b.t: A verb in a dictionary appears in the infinitive, the "to…" form. Almost all German infinitives end in -en: kommen (to come), wohnen (to live), heißen (to be called), lernen (to learn). To use the verb in a sentence you remove -en to get the stem and add an ending that matches the subject.
Look at the patterns, they make the table easy to learn:
• wir, sie (they) and Sie always use the infinitive form. Three of the seven forms need no thinking at all.
• er/sie/es and ihr both end in -t.
• ich is the only form that ends in -e.
Achtung: Don't write "ich kommen". English speakers often keep the infinitive for every person. German needs the ending: ich komme, du kommst, er kommt.

pages.t: K2 · 2.4 Verbs: the infinitive, the stem and the endings (2)

b.t: sein is the most important German verb, and it is irregular: its forms do not follow the stem + ending pattern. You must simply learn them by heart, and you will use them every day.
Use sein for who or what someone is, for origin, for descriptions and for age:
Ich bin Student.
Raj ist nicht müde.
Wir sind aus Deutschland.
Ich bin vierundzwanzig (Jahre alt).
Wie alt bist du?
Merke: No article before a profession. German says Ich bin Student (not "ein Student") and Sie ist Lehrerin. Female forms usually add -in: der Student → die Studentin, der Lehrer → die Lehrerin.

German has two kinds of questions. The word order is different for each.
Questions with a question word (W-questions)
Question words start with w-, so they are easy to remember. The verb comes immediately after the question word, in second position.
Wie heißt du?
Woher kommen Sie?
Wo wohnst du?
Wer ist das?
Wie alt sind Sie?

Englisch ↔ Deutsch: English how and German wie look alike but are not always the same: you ask for someone's name with wie (Wie heißt du?), literally "How are you called?". Don't say Was ist dein Name? when you can say Wie heißt du?; both are correct, but the second is much more natural.
Yes/no questions
If the answer is ja or nein, the verb comes first. There is no extra word like English "do".
Kommst du aus Indien?
Wohnen Sie in Berlin?
Sind Sie Herr Patel?
Ist Anna müde?
You can answer in full or briefly: Ja, ich komme aus Indien. or just Ja. If the answer is no: Nein, ich komme aus Deutschland.

In a normal German statement the conjugated verb is always in second position. That means second position in the sentence, not necessarily the second word. The first position can hold the subject or something else. When something other than the subject comes first, the subject moves behind the verb.
Both Ich wohne in Berlin and In Berlin wohne ich mean the same thing. The second is slightly more emphatic: "It's in Berlin that I live."
Merke: Verb second. In statements and in W-questions the conjugated verb stands in position 2. In yes/no questions it stands in position 1.
Saying "not": nicht
Nicht negates the verb or the whole statement and normally goes at the end:
Ich komme nicht aus Indien.
Ich arbeite heute nicht.
Anna ist nicht müde.
When you simply contradict a statement, you can also answer with nein: Kommst du aus China? – Nein, ich komme nicht aus China. The word kein ("no / not a") is introduced in chapter 3.

b.t: Where I am from, where I live, what I speak
Three small patterns give you a lot of conversational power:

r: Ich komme aus Indien. Ich komme aus Hamburg.

After aus and in they need the dative case, which you will learn properly later in the book; for now just copy the whole phrase: aus der Schweiz, aus den USA, in der Schweiz, in den USA.
Ich komme aus Österreich.
Sie kommt aus der Schweiz.
Wir wohnen in den USA.
Er spricht Spanisch und Französisch.

pages.t: K3 · 3.2 Nouns: capital letters and genders

b.t: Every noun is written with a capital letter, wherever it appears in the sentence: der Tisch, die Lampe, das Buch, Ich habe einen Bruder. This is a gift for the reader: you can see the nouns at a glance.
Every noun also has a grammatical gender: masculine, feminine or neuter. The gender is shown by the definite article, the German "the":

r: der Tisch, der Mann, der Vater
die Lampe, die Frau, die Mutter
das Buch, das Kind, das Haus
die Tische, die Lampen, die Bücher

b.t: Gender is a property of the word, not of the thing. A table is not masculine in any real sense; the word Tisch just happens to be masculine, and das Mädchen ("the girl") is neuter. English speakers find this strange, but there is a payoff: once you know a noun's gender, the rest of the sentence follows from it.
The golden rule for learning nouns

Merke: Always learn a noun together with its article and plural: der Tisch, -e; die Lampe, -n; das Buch, ¨-er. Never learn "Tisch" on its own. This book writes every noun that way and colours the article: der blue, die red, das green.
Rules of thumb for gender

pages.t: K3 · 3.2 Nouns: capital letters and genders (2)

b.t: For many nouns there is no rule and you must memorise the article. But a surprising number follow patterns. These rules are very reliable:

r: People and animals follow their natural sex
der Vater, die Mutter, der Bruder, die Schwester, der Mann, die Frau
Compound nouns take the gender of the last part
der Kühlschrank (der Schrank), die Freizeit (die Zeit), das Handyfoto (das Foto)
die Wohnung (flat), die Einladung (invitation), die Möglichkeit (possibility)
die Lehrerin, die Freundin, die Studentin
die Lampe, die Katze, die Tasche, die Schule
das Auto, das Foto, das Kino

b.t: Several exceptions are worth knowing from the start: das Kind and das Baby (young people and animals are neuter), der Kaffee, der Tee, der Name (they look like "-e" nouns but are masculine).
If no rule applies, the safest guess is der, because masculine nouns are slightly more frequent. It is only a guess, so check the glossary.
der, die or das?

b.t: Use the rules of thumb to choose the article. The English meaning is in brackets.
The indefinite article is German "a / an". It also shows gender:
Notice that **masculine and neuter both use ein. Only the feminine adds -e**: eine. There is no plural of ein: ein Tisch becomes just Tische ("tables"), without an article.
The basic question-and-answer pair for everything around you is:
Was ist das? – Das ist ein Tisch.
b.g: What is that? – That is a table.

b.t: Was ist das? – Das ist eine Lampe.
b.g: What is that? – That is a lamp.

b.t: Was ist das? – Das ist ein Buch.
b.g: What is that? – That is a book.

b.t: Das ist ein Hund. Der Hund heißt Rex.
b.g: That is a dog. The dog is called Rex.

b.t: Note how the second sentence uses the definite article (der Hund): you introduce something new with ein/eine, and then, once it is known, you refer to it with der/die/das. English does the same ("a dog … the dog").

The plural article is always die, whatever the gender. The plural noun itself changes in one of several ways. There are five endings and an optional umlaut (a → ä, o → ö, u → ü, au → äu):

r: der Tisch → die Tische; der Stuhl → die Stühle; der Hund → die Hunde
das Kind → die Kinder; das Buch → die Bücher; das Haus → die Häuser
die Lampe → die Lampen; die Katze → die Katzen; die Frau → die Frauen
das Auto → die Autos; das Handy → die Handys; das Foto → die Fotos
words from other languages, ending in a vowel
das Zimmer → die Zimmer; der Bruder → die Brüder; das Fenster → die Fenster

b.t: Merke: Plural shortcuts that cover most nouns: - Feminine → almost always -n / -en (die Lampe → die Lampen, die Tür → die Türen). - Nouns ending in -e → add -n (die Katze → die Katzen, der Junge → die Jungen). - Foreign words and many short words ending in a vowel → -s (das Auto → die Autos). - Nouns ending in -er, -el, -en → usually no ending, sometimes with an umlaut (das Zimmer → die Zimmer, der Bruder → die Brüder).
This book writes the plural after the noun in the vocabulary lists: -e, ¨-e (umlaut + e), -er, ¨-er, -n, -en, -s, - (no change), ¨- (umlaut only). Learn it with the noun.
Some nouns only exist in the singular (das Wasser, das Internet) and some only in the plural: die Eltern (parents), die Leute (people), die Geschwister (siblings).
Write the plural

After sein, haben is the second most important verb. It is irregular in the du and er/sie/es forms (the b disappears):
Ich habe eine Schwester.
Hast du Geschwister?
Anna hat einen Bruder.
Wir haben keine Kinder.
Haben is also used in many fixed phrases where English uses "be": Hunger haben (to be hungry), Durst haben (to be thirsty), Zeit haben (to have time).

pages.t: K3 · 3.6 The object: the accusative case

b.t: In Ich habe einen Bruder the word for "brother" is not ein Bruder but einen Bruder. That is the accusative case, the form used for the direct object: the person or thing that the action is directed at. Both haben and many other verbs (sehen, brauchen, kaufen, lieben) take an accusative object.
Here is the best news about the accusative: only the masculine changes.
Both changes add an -n: der → den, ein → einen. Everything else stays exactly as it is.
Ich habe einen Bruder.
Ich habe eine Schwester.
Ich habe ein Kind.
Ich sehe den Hund.
Ich sehe die Katze.
Ich brauche einen Stuhl.

Achtung: A common beginner error: "Ich habe ein Bruder." The brother is the object of haben, so the masculine article becomes einen. Say it aloud a few times: ich habe einen Bruder, einen Hund, einen Tisch.

German has two negations, and choosing the right one is easy once you know the rule.
• kein negates a noun that has ein/eine or no article: Ich habe ein Auto → Ich habe kein Auto.
• nicht negates everything else: verbs, adjectives, places, nouns with der/die/das or mein/dein.

r: Das ist ein Hund. → Das ist kein Hund. · Ich habe Zeit. → Ich habe keine Zeit.
Ich arbeite nicht. · Anna ist nicht müde.
Das ist nicht der Hund. · Das ist nicht mein Bruder.

b.t: kein takes the same endings as ein: kein / keine / kein, and in the accusative masculine keinen. The plural is keine.
Das ist kein Hund.
Ich habe keine Katze.
Ich habe keinen Bruder.
Wir haben keine Kinder.
Ich bin nicht müde.

Another small word that helps: answering a negative question. If someone asks Hast du keine Schwester? ("Don't you have a sister?"), the German doch means "yes, I do": Doch, ich habe eine Schwester. And nein means "no, I don't". English has no one-word equivalent.

pages.t: K3 · 3.8 mein, dein: my and your

b.t: Possessive words ("my, your, his…") take the same endings as ein / kein: no ending for masculine and neuter, -e for feminine and plural, and -en for masculine accusative.
The other possessives (sein, ihr, unser, euer, Ihr) follow the same pattern and are introduced in later chapters.
Das ist mein Vater.
Das ist meine Mutter.
Meine Eltern wohnen in Hamburg.
Wie heißt dein Bruder?

b.g: I get up at seven o'clock every day.

b.g: At half past seven I have breakfast: I eat a bread roll and drink a coffee.

b.t: Days, months and seasons are nouns, so they are written with a capital letter. All of them are masculine: der Montag, der Juli, der Sommer. (The only common exception is das Wochenende, the weekend.)
Merke: The week begins on Monday in German calendars. Saturday is Samstag in most of the country, and Sonnabend in parts of northern and eastern Germany. In the south you hear Samstag.

Four little prepositions do almost all the work. am (= an dem) and im (= in dem) are contractions that use the dative (you will meet it properly in chapter 7); for now just learn the fixed phrases. um (clock times) and von … bis have no article to worry about:

r: days and parts of the day
am Montag, am Morgen, am Abend, am Wochenende
um acht Uhr, um halb zwei

b.t: An exception to remember: in der Nacht ("at night"), not am Nacht, because die Nacht is feminine.
Am Montag habe ich Deutschkurs.
b.g: On Monday I have German class.

b.t: Im Sommer fahre ich nach Italien.
b.g: In summer I go to Italy.

b.t: Wir arbeiten von Montag bis Freitag.
b.g: We work from Monday to Friday.

Adding -s to a day turns it into "on …s" (every Monday): montags, dienstags. Parts of the day work the same way: morgens, mittags, abends, nachts.
Today, tomorrow, yesterday
heute (today), morgen (tomorrow), gestern (yesterday). Morgen is both "tomorrow" (lower case, adverb) and "morning" (capital, noun): morgen früh means "tomorrow morning".
You ask: Wie spät ist es? or Wie viel Uhr ist es? And Um wie viel Uhr …? asks "At what time?".
The official way (24 hours)
Radio, train stations and timetables use the 24-hour clock: hours + Uhr + minutes.
Es ist acht Uhr.
Es ist dreizehn Uhr fünfzehn.
Der Zug fährt um achtzehn Uhr dreißig.
Der Film beginnt um zwanzig Uhr.
The everyday way (12 hours)
In conversation, Germans use the "past / to" system with nach (past) and vor (to), plus Viertel (quarter) and halb (half):

Achtung: halb acht is 7:30, not 8:30. Halb looks forward to the next hour: "half (way to) eight". Most learners read halb acht as 8:30 because English "half past eight" is 8:30. (British "half seven" means 7:30, but that is a different number from German halb acht.) Think "half an hour before eight".
Tipp: When you do not catch a time, ask Wie spät ist es? and then repeat it back with um: Um halb acht, richtig? ("At half past seven, right?"). It is the quickest way to avoid missing a train.

Many German verbs have a prefix that detaches and goes to the end of the sentence. These are trennbare Verben, "separable verbs". They look like one word in the dictionary (aufstehen, to get up) and split when you use them in the present tense:

r: Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.
Der Kurs fängt um neun Uhr an.

b.t: The rule is the same one you already know: the conjugated verb stays in position 2, and the prefix goes to the very end. The sentence is held together like a bracket, the Satzklammer:
Ich stehe jeden Tag um sieben Uhr auf.
verb (2nd position) … … … prefix (last)
The prefix always sits at the end of a statement, however long the sentence becomes. In yes/no questions the verb comes first and the prefix is still last: Stehst du früh auf?
How do I know if a prefix separates?

Prefixes that are words on their own, mostly prepositions and adverbs, separate: an-, auf-, aus-, ein-, mit-, vor-, zu-, ab-, fern-, zurück-. A second group of prefixes never separates: be-, ge-, er-, ver-, zer-, ent-. Those verbs behave like any other verb: Ich verstehe dich. Ich bekomme einen Brief.
A useful clue is stress: in a separable verb the stress is on the prefix (AUFstehen), in an inseparable verb it is on the stem (beKOMmen).
Ich stehe früh auf.
Wann fängt der Film an?
Er ruft seine Eltern an.
Kommst du mit?
Wir kaufen heute nicht ein.
Ich verstehe das nicht.

b.t: möchten is the polite way to say what you want. It is a modal verb (chapter 9 explains the whole family). Its forms:
Notice that ich and er/sie/es are the same (no ending -t), like all modal verbs. It works in two ways:

1. With a noun in the accusative: Ich möchte einen Kaffee. 2. With an infinitive at the end of the sentence: Ich möchte einen Kaffee trinken. The infinitive goes to the end, just like a separable prefix.
Was möchten Sie?

Möchtest du Zucker?
Wir möchten bitte zahlen.
Anna möchte Kuchen essen.

b.t: Three ways to say what you like.
1. mögen, "to like", is another modal verb, used with a noun: Ich mag Käse. Er mag keinen Fisch. (Forms: ich mag, du magst, er mag, wir mögen, ihr mögt, sie mögen.)
2. gern is placed after the verb and means "with pleasure", so any verb can "like": Ich esse gern Pizza. Ich trinke gern Tee. Its negative is nicht gern.
3. Comparison: gern → lieber → am liebsten (like, prefer, like best):
Ich esse gern Schokolade.
Isst du gern Fisch?
Nein, ich esse nicht gern Fisch.
b.g: No, I don't like eating fish.

b.t: Ich trinke lieber Tee als Kaffee.
Am liebsten esse ich Pizza.
b.g: I like pizza best of all.

b.t: Ich mag keinen Kaffee.

Englisch ↔ Deutsch: English "I like to eat pizza" becomes German "I eat gladly pizza". German does not use a separate "like" verb for activities: you take the verb you need (essen, trinken, lesen) and add gern. Ich mag essen Pizza is a common mistake.

pages.t: K5 · 5.6 es gibt: there is, there are

b.t: Es gibt + accusative means "there is / there are". It is always singular (gibt), whatever follows. You use it to ask what a place has, and to say what is available:
Gibt es hier ein Café?
Es gibt Kuchen und Kaffee.
Heute gibt es keine Suppe.
Was gibt es zum Mittagessen?

Hundreds work like the tens: hundert, zweihundert, dreihundert … and tausend (1000). The smaller number follows without und: hundertzwanzig (120), zweihundertfünfundfünfzig (255). Everything is one word.
Prices say the euros and the cents: elf Euro fünfzig (11,50 €). Germans write a comma where English writes a point.
The question is Was kostet das? or Wie viel kostet das? (one thing) and Was kosten die Brötchen? (several).

Water in restaurants is not free and it comes with a choice: still (without bubbles) or mit Kohlensäure (sparkling). b.t: To point at an item, use dieser / diese / dieses, "this" (and the plural diese). They change like the definite article der / die / das, so you already know the pattern. In the accusative only the masculine changes (diesen):

When you already know what you are talking about, you can drop the noun: Diese hier! ("This one here!"), Den da. ("That one there.").
In Ich sehe den Hund the word den Hund is the object. When the dog is already known, you replace it with a pronoun, in English "I see him". In German these are the accusative pronouns:

pages.t: K7 · 7.4 Where is it? The dative case

b.t: So far you know two cases: the nominative (the subject) and the accusative (the direct object). To say where something is, German uses the dative case after position words. You can recognise it at once because the articles change:

Two things to notice. Masculine and neuter are the same (dem, einem), and **feminine is der / einer, which looks like the masculine nominative but is not. In the plural the noun itself usually takes -n**: die Zimmer → in den Zimmern, die Kinder → mit den Kindern. (If the plural already ends in -n or -s, nothing is added: den Autos.)
Two-way prepositions
Nine prepositions can take the accusative or the dative: an, auf, hinter, in, neben, über, unter, vor, zwischen. The question decides which:
In this chapter you only need the Wo? side: dative.

b.t: (And for "let's": Gehen wir!, the infinitive followed by wir.)
• Sie keeps the pronoun, which comes after the verb: Nehmen Sie die U-Bahn. Fahren Sie hier ab.
• du drops the pronoun and the -st: du gehst → Geh!, du kommst → Komm!. Add bitte to be polite.
• Stem-changing verbs keep the vowel change from the du form: du nimmst → Nimm!, du sprichst → Sprich langsam!, du liest → Lies! (But a→ä does not carry over: du fährst → Fahr!)
• Separable verbs put the prefix at the end: Steh auf! Kommen Sie mit!

b.t: Anna and Raj make plans for the weekend. Each sentence has two verbs: a small helper (kannst, möchte, muss, wollen) in second place and a second verb at the very end (mitkommen, gehen, arbeiten). That is the structure of this chapter.
Anna and Raj are talking after class on Friday.
Anna: Hast du am Samstag Zeit? Wir wollen ins Kino gehen.
b.g: Do you have time on Saturday? We want to go to the cinema.

b.t: Raj: Leider kann ich nicht. Ich muss arbeiten.
b.g: Unfortunately I can't. I have to work.

b.t: Anna: Schade! Und am Sonntag?
Raj: Am Sonntag habe ich frei. Was möchtest du machen?
b.g: On Sunday I'm off. What would you like to do?

b.t: Anna: Wir können im Park Fußball spielen. Kannst du Fußball spielen?

German has three ways to say what you do for fun:

r: spielen + sport or game or instrument

Ich schwimme, tanze, singe, wandere, lese, koche.
Ich höre Musik. Ich sehe Filme. Ich treffe Freunde. Ich fahre Rad.

b.t: To say what you like, add gern (chapter 5): Ich schwimme gern. Ich höre gern Musik. Ask a friend: Was machst du in deiner Freizeit? and Was sind deine Hobbys?

Modal verbs (Modalverben) are helper verbs that say whether something is possible, allowed, necessary or wanted. You already know möchten (chapter 5). The full family:
Their forms in the present tense:
Look at the patterns:
• ich and er/sie/es are always identical, and carry no ending: ich kann, er kann.
• The singular has a different vowel from the plural: können → kann, müssen → muss, dürfen → darf, wollen → will. The plural, and the infinitive, are regular.
• sollen has no vowel change.
The second verb goes to the end
The modal is the conjugated verb, so it stays in position 2. The main verb goes to the very end, in the infinitive:
Ich kann heute nicht kommen.
Wir wollen am Wochenende ins Kino gehen.
Darf ich hier sitzen?
This is the same bracket you saw with separable verbs. With a separable verb, the infinitive is written as one word: Ich muss früh aufstehen. (not "auf stehen").

Merke: Modal + infinitive at the end. The modal verb is conjugated and in position 2 (or position 1 in a yes/no question). The other verb stays in the infinitive and goes to the end: Ich möchte Deutsch lernen. Kannst du mich anrufen? Wir müssen jetzt gehen.
You can leave the infinitive out when it is obvious: Ich kann Deutsch. (= Ich kann Deutsch sprechen.), Ich muss nach Hause. (= ... gehen).

r: Ich kann Gitarre spielen. Kannst du mir helfen?
Ich will heute Abend ins Kino.
Darf ich fragen? Hier darf man nicht parken.

b.t: An ordinal number says the order: first, second, third. They end in -te up to 19 and -ste from 20:
Spot the irregulars: erste, dritte, siebte, achte. In writing, an ordinal is a number with a full stop: 1., 2., 3.

The date. Der Wievielte ist heute? ("What's the date?") is answered with Heute ist der + ordinal: Heute ist der 28. Oktober. ("Today is the twenty-eighth of October.") Am is used for "on": am 3. Mai = am dritten Mai. And for birthdays: Wann hast du Geburtstag? – Am 14. Juli.
Dates are written day.month.year: 03.05.2027 or 3. Mai 2027. Years are said as hundreds: 1999 = neunzehnhundertneunundneunzig, 2027 = zweitausendsiebenundzwanzig.

Merke: - Modal verbs: können, wollen, müssen, dürfen, sollen, möchten (and mögen). ich and er/sie/es have no ending: ich kann, er kann. Singular vowel: kann, will, muss, darf. - Modal + infinitive at the end: Ich muss heute arbeiten. Kannst du mitkommen? - nicht müssen = don't have to. nicht dürfen = must not. - Hobbies: spielen + sport or instrument; gern for liking. - Invitations: Hast du Lust …? Wollen wir …? Kultur: Landeskunde: free time. Germans spend a lot of free time in clubs (Vereine): there are sports clubs for football, handball, swimming, gym and many more, and also music, chess and choir clubs. A Spaziergang (walk) on Sunday is traditional, and hiking (Wandern) is a national pastime in the Alps and low mountain ranges. Meetings with friends are usually planned in advance: an invitation without a time or place is not complete. Birthdays are celebrated with a cake and the host usually invites guests, not the other way round.

German weather words nearly all use es: the "it" with no real meaning, as in English "it rains". Because es is just a placeholder, the verb stays in the er/sie/es form.

r: Wie ist das Wetter? (What is the weather like?)
Es ist sonnig / warm / kalt / windig / bewölkt.
Es regnet. (It is raining.) Es schneit. (It is snowing.)
Die Sonne scheint. (The sun is shining.) Der Wind weht.
Es sind zwanzig Grad. / Es hat fünf Grad.

b.t: Temperatures: plus and minus: Es sind minus drei Grad. Es ist null Grad. Wetter (weather) is das Wetter, die Wettervorhersage is the forecast.
Wie ist das Wetter in Hamburg?

b.t: Heute regnet es, aber morgen scheint die Sonne.

b.t: Im Winter schneit es oft.
Es sind zwölf Grad.
Im Sommer ist es warm und sonnig.

b.t: Zum Glück regnet es nicht.

b.t: On Monday morning, Anna asks Raj about his weekend. The answers are in the past. Look at every sentence: there are always two verb parts, a form of haben or sein in second position, and a participle at the end (gemacht, gegessen, gefahren).
Monday morning before class.
Anna: Hallo Raj! Was hast du am Wochenende gemacht?
b.g: Hi Raj! What did you do at the weekend?

b.t: Raj: Am Samstag habe ich lange geschlafen. Dann habe ich Wäsche gewaschen und eingekauft.
b.g: On Saturday I slept late. Then I did laundry and went shopping.

b.t: Anna: Und am Sonntag?
Raj: Am Sonntag bin ich mit Freunden an den See gefahren. Wir haben Fußball gespielt und gegrillt.
b.g: On Sunday I went to the lake with friends. We played football and had a barbecue.

b.t: Anna: Wie schön! Wart ihr den ganzen Tag dort?
b.g: How nice! Were you there all day?

b.t: Raj: Ja, wir sind um zehn Uhr gekommen und um sieben nach Hause gegangen. Ich war sehr müde.

b.t: Anna: Ich habe leider gearbeitet. Ich hatte keine Zeit.
b.g: I unfortunately worked. I had no time.

pages.t: K11 · 11.2 How the perfect tense works

b.t: German has several past tenses. In everyday speech and messages you use the Perfekt, built from two parts:
haben / sein (conjugated, position 2) + participle (Partizip II, at the end)
Ich habe gestern Fußball gespielt.
Wir sind nach Berlin gefahren.
The helper verb is conjugated. The participle never changes. And the participle goes to the end of the sentence, the same bracket as with modal verbs and separable verbs.
The perfect covers all English past forms: Ich habe gearbeitet means "I worked", "I have worked" and "I was working".
Forming the participle
Regular (weak) verbs: ge- + stem + -t
If the stem ends in -t or -d, add an -e-: arbeiten → gearbeitet.
Irregular (strong) verbs: ge- + stem (often changed) + -en

pages.t: K11 · 11.2 How the perfect tense works (2)

b.t: Strong verbs have to be learned with their participle. That is why the vocabulary lists in this chapter show the participle.
Separable verbs: the ge- goes in the middle
The participle puts ge between the prefix and the stem, written as one word: aufstehen → aufgestanden, einkaufen → eingekauft, anrufen → angerufen, fernsehen → ferngesehen, mitkommen → mitgekommen.
Inseparable prefixes and -ieren verbs: no ge- at all

Verbs with the prefixes be-, ge-, er-, ver-, zer-, ent- and verbs ending in -ieren do not add ge-: besuchen → besucht, bezahlen → bezahlt, verstehen → verstanden, telefonieren → telefoniert, studieren → studiert.

pages.t: K11 · 11.2 How the perfect tense works (3)

b.t: Merke: Check the first letters of the verb. If it starts with be-, ge-, er-, ver-, ent-, zer- or ends in -ieren, there is no ge-. If it is separable, the ge goes between prefix and stem. Otherwise, ge- comes first.
Ich habe Fußball gespielt.
Wir haben Pizza gegessen.
Er hat seine Mutter angerufen.
Sie ist früh aufgestanden.
b.g: She got up early. (aufstehen uses sein)

b.t: Ich habe das nicht verstanden.
Wir haben ein Zimmer reserviert.

Most verbs use haben. A smaller group uses sein: verbs of movement from A to B and verbs of a change of state, plus sein and bleiben:

r: gehen (ist gegangen), fahren (ist gefahren), kommen (ist gekommen), fliegen (ist geflogen)
everything else, including all verbs with an object
hat gemacht, hat gegessen, hat gekauft, hat gearbeitet, hat gelesen

b.t: A quick test: if the verb answers Wohin? (where to?) or means "become", try sein. If it takes a direct object (Ich habe einen Kaffee getrunken) it is haben.
Ich bin nach Berlin gefahren.
Wir sind um acht aufgestanden.
Sie ist zu Hause geblieben.
Er ist gestern angekommen.
Ich habe einen Film gesehen.
Wir haben Deutsch gelernt.

Achtung: Don't use sein with every verb of movement in English. You say Ich bin gefahren (I went by vehicle) but Ich habe ein Auto gefahren is also possible when fahren takes an object. At A1, learn: gehen, fahren, kommen, fliegen, bleiben, aufstehen, sein with sein, and everything else with haben.

Merke: - Perfekt = haben / sein (position 2) + participle (end). It translates every English past form. - Regular verbs: ge- + stem + -t (gemacht, gelernt, gearbeitet). - Strong verbs: ge- + stem + -en, often with a vowel change (gegessen, getrunken, geschrieben, gegangen). Learn them with the participle. - Separable: ge in the middle (aufgestanden, eingekauft, angerufen). - No ge-: be-, ge-, er-, ver-, ent-, zer- and -ieren (besucht, verstanden, telefoniert). - sein for movement and change of state (gegangen, gefahren, gekommen, geblieben, aufgestanden) and for sein itself; haben for the rest. - war / hatte for sein / haben, schon / noch nicht for already / not yet.

Kultur: Landeskunde: spoken and written German. In Germany you hear Ich habe gegessen but you read er aß in a novel. In southern Germany, Austria and Switzerland people use the Perfekt even more, and often avoid the Präteritum altogether, except for war and hatte. The word gestern is useful in any context, and so are vorgestern (the day before yesterday) and heute Morgen (this morning).

b.t: Since chapter 7 you know the dative case for nouns. Now the pronouns in the dative:
Now you know why Wie geht es dir? has dir, not du: the verb gehen in this phrase takes a dative person ("how goes it to you?"). That is also why mir appears in Es geht mir gut.
Verbs that take a dative object
A small group of common verbs has a dative object (the person who benefits or is affected), not an accusative:
Notice how the meaning turns around from English: Das Hemd gefällt mir = "The shirt is pleasing to me" = "I like the shirt". The thing liked is the subject (nominative), the person is the dative.

Merke: - Jobs: Ich bin Lehrer. (no article), Ich arbeite als Koch / bei Siemens / in einem Büro. Women: -in. - Dative pronouns: mir, dir, ihm, ihr, ihm, uns, euch, ihnen, Ihnen. Wie geht es dir? Es geht mir gut. - Dative verbs: helfen, gefallen, gehören, danken, schmecken, passen, wehtun. The person is dative: Das Hemd gefällt mir. - Health: Ich habe Kopfschmerzen. Mir tut der Kopf weh. Kultur: Landeskunde: work and health. In Germany nearly everyone has health insurance (Krankenversicherung) and shows an insurance card at the doctor's. You usually need an appointment (Termin); in emergencies, 112 is the number for the fire brigade and ambulance, and 110 is for the police. If you are ill and cannot work, your employer expects a doctor's note (Krankmeldung). Pharmacies (Apotheken) are marked with a red letter A, and one is always open at night in each area (Notdienst). At work, colleagues use Sie and surnames at first; many workplaces move to du and first names once people know each other.

The next level, A2, builds on exactly the foundation you have now. In A2 you will work on:
• Subordinate clauses with weil, dass, wenn, obwohl (verb at the end of the clause).
• Adjective endings (ein großer Tisch, die kleine Katze).
• Comparison (größer, am größten, besser, am besten).
• Reflexive verbs (sich freuen, sich treffen) and more separable verbs.
• The genitive (das Auto meines Bruders), relative clauses (der Mann, der …) and the future with werden.
• Connected writing: emails, descriptions, opinions.

Merke: You have completed A1. If you can do the tasks in 13.4 without much help, you are ready for the Goethe-Zertifikat A1 and for A2. If a section felt hard, don't push on: go back to its chapter, repeat the worksheets and review the vocabulary with the flashcards. Finally, speak. Even five minutes a day of reading aloud will change how you sound.

Kultur: Landeskunde: the Goethe-Zertifikat A1. The Goethe-Institut's A1 exam, Start Deutsch 1, is accepted by embassies for family reunification in Germany. It has four parts of 25 points each, 100 points in total, and you pass with 60 (and all four parts taken). The exam takes about 80 minutes. Examination centres exist all over the world, and there are alternative certificates from telc and ÖSD. Whatever exam you choose, the best preparation is the same: listen, read, write and speak a little every day.
